content.text: The gravitational field strength acting on a spacecraft decreases as its altitude increases. This is due to a change in the
mass of Earth.
mass of the spacecraft.
density of the atmosphere.
distance of the spacecraft from Earth's centre.
Write the expression for the gravitational field strength of a body of mass $M$ at a point a distance $r$ from its centre, and identify every quantity in it.
Then ask which of those quantities is changing as the spacecraft's altitude increases.
D

The field strength depends only on the mass $M$ of Earth and the distance $r$ from its centre. As the altitude of the spacecraft increases, $r$ increases while $M$ stays constant, and $g = GM/r^{2}$ therefore falls.

items: The mass of Earth does not change.
The mass of the spacecraft is not in the expression for the field strength at all.
The density of the atmosphere has no effect on a gravitational field.

1 mark: selects option D, recognising that the gravitational field strength at a point depends on the distance from the centre of the source mass ($g = GM/r^{2}$), which increases as the spacecraft's altitude increases

content.text: The energy lost in a transmission line is $I^{2}R$, so the line current must be kept as small as possible.
For a given transmitted power, a small current means a large voltage. So the voltage has to be raised before transmission and lowered again at the houses.
Check the order of the transformers in each diagram as well as the labels on the line: the step-up belongs at the power station.
C

Raising the transmission voltage therefore reduces the current and the energy wasted as heat in the lines. The transformer at the power station must step the voltage up (and the current down) for transmission, and a second, step-down transformer must reduce the voltage to household values at the houses.
That is the third diagram, which shows a step-up transformer at the power station, a high voltage and low current on the transmission line, and a step-down transformer at the houses.

The fourth diagram has the transformers in the right order but labels the transmission line as high current and low voltage, which contradicts the step-up transformer shown.

content.text: Which of the following best represents the expected pattern on the screen?

content.alt_text: All four answer patterns for the double-slit question drawn as one image, labelled A, B, C and D down the page. A shows a single broad bright band; B shows two bright bands; C shows three bright bands of equal intensity; D shows four bright bands, each progressively wider and fainter. This image carries the patterns for options A, B, C and D and is attached to option A only.

content.text: Screen pattern: a single bright band only, with no dark bands, and the bright band is widest at the centre.
Screen pattern: a series of many equally spaced bright fringes of equal intensity separated by dark fringes, with the spacing of the fringes uniform across the screen.
Screen pattern: two bright fringes only, one either side of a wide dark central band, with the fringes curved rather than straight.
Light from each slit spreads out as circular wavefronts, so the two sets of waves overlap everywhere on the screen.
Where the two waves arrive in phase they reinforce; where they arrive half a wavelength out of step they cancel. This repeats regularly as you move across the screen.
The path difference changes at a constant rate across the screen, so the bright and dark fringes must be equally spaced and of equal width. Count and measure the bands in each option.
C

Constructive and destructive interference occur wherever the path difference from the two slits is a whole number, or a half number, of wavelengths. Because the path difference grows steadily with position on the screen, the fringes are equally spaced and equally wide.
The correct pattern is therefore a series of evenly spaced bright bands separated by dark bands, which is the third option.

items: The first pattern (one broad band) and the second (two bands) show far too few fringes.
The fourth pattern shows bands of unequal width and unequal spacing, which cannot come from a path difference that changes uniformly.
1 mark: selects option C, the pattern of regularly spaced bright and dark interference fringes of equal intensity, as produced by constructive and destructive interference of light from the two slits

content.text: Caesium-137 has a half-life of 30 years. What mass of caesium-137 will remain after 90 years, if the initial mass was $120\,\mathrm{g}$?
$4\,\mathrm{g}$
$15\,\mathrm{g}$
$40\,\mathrm{g}$
$60\,\mathrm{g}$
Work out how many half-lives have elapsed by dividing the elapsed time by the half-life.
Halve the mass once for each half-life, and write the sequence down as you go so the number of halvings is obvious.
Check your result against the other options: a distractor is often what you get from the wrong number of halvings.
B
Halving step by step: $120\,\mathrm{g} \rightarrow 60\,\mathrm{g} \rightarrow 30\,\mathrm{g} \rightarrow 15\,\mathrm{g}$ after 90 years.

items: $60\,\mathrm{g}$ is the mass after only one half-life and $30\,\mathrm{g}$ after two.
$4\,\mathrm{g}$ corresponds to about five halvings, far longer than 90 years.
1 mark: selects option B, i.e. recognises that 90 years is three half-lives so that $120 \rightarrow 60 \rightarrow 30 \rightarrow 15\,\mathrm{g}$

content.text: An exoplanet is in an elliptical orbit, moving in the direction shown. The distances between consecutive positions P, Q, R and S are equal.

content.alt_text: Left half of an elliptical orbit diagram: the left end of the ellipse with the marked points R (upper) and Q (lower) and a small star symbol labelled 'Star' inside the ellipse near the left focus.

content.text: Between which two points is the exoplanet's travel time the greatest?
P and Q
Q and R
R and S
S and P
Kepler's second law: the line joining the planet to the star sweeps out equal areas in equal times.
This means the planet must move slowest where it is furthest from the star, at the far end of the ellipse, and fastest where it is closest.
The star sits at the focus on the left of the ellipse. All four arcs are equal in length, so compare them by how far each one lies from that focus.
D

content.latex: \frac{\Delta A}{\Delta t} = \text{constant} \;\Rightarrow\; v \propto \frac{1}{r^{2}} \text{ at equal } \Delta A

content.text: The star is at the left focus. Since equal areas are swept out in equal times, the planet's speed is lowest at the far (right-hand) end of the ellipse, where it is furthest from the star, and highest at the near (left-hand) end.

The direction of travel is S to P, then P to Q, then Q to R, then R to S. Of these four equal arcs, S to P is the one at the far end of the ellipse, so it is covered most slowly and takes the longest time.

items: Q to R spans the near end, close to the focus, where the planet is moving fastest, so that is the shortest time.
P to Q and R to S lie along the top and bottom of the ellipse at intermediate distances, so their times lie between the two extremes.

1 mark: selects option D, recognising that by the law of equal areas the planet moves most slowly where it is furthest from the star, so the greatest travel time is for the equal arc closest to the aphelion (S and P)

content.text: An electron would produce an electromagnetic wave when it is
stationary.
in a stable hydrogen atom.
moving at a constant velocity.
moving at a constant speed in a circular path.
Electromagnetic waves are produced by oscillating, that is accelerating, charges.
Be precise about 'constant': constant velocity means no acceleration, but constant speed does not. A charge can keep the same speed while its direction of travel changes continuously.
Work through the four situations and ask in each one whether the charge's velocity is changing.
D
An accelerating charge radiates an electromagnetic wave. The test in each case is whether the charge's velocity is changing.

items: Stationary: the velocity is zero and unchanging, so there is no acceleration and no radiation.
In a stable hydrogen atom: by definition the electron is not moving between energy states, so it is not accelerating.
Moving at constant velocity: neither the speed nor the direction changes, so the acceleration is zero.
Moving at constant speed in a circular path: the direction of the velocity changes continuously, so the velocity is changing and the charge is accelerating.

content.text: Only the circular motion involves an acceleration, so only that case produces an electromagnetic wave.

items: 1 mark: selects option D, recognising that an electromagnetic wave is produced by an accelerating charge; a charge moving at constant speed in a circular path has a continually changing velocity, so it is accelerating

content.text: A proton and a neutron travel at the same speed. Which statement correctly explains the difference between their de Broglie wavelengths?
The proton has a longer wavelength because its mass is greater.
The proton has a shorter wavelength because its mass is smaller.
The neutron has a shorter wavelength because its mass is greater.
The neutron has a longer wavelength because its mass is smaller.
The de Broglie wavelength of a particle is $\lambda = h/p = h/(mv)$.
The two particles travel at the same speed and both have the same momentum per unit mass, so the mass is the only thing left to compare.
Do not forget that the neutron is slightly heavier than the proton even though both are electrically neutral.
C

At equal speed the de Broglie wavelength is inversely proportional to the mass. The neutron is the heavier particle, $m_n \approx 1.675\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$ against $m_p \approx 1.673\times10^{-27}\,\mathrm{kg}$, so the neutron has the shorter wavelength.

items: The first option names the proton as the longer wavelength and the greater mass, but the greater mass gives the shorter wavelength.
The second and fourth options claim the neutron is the lighter particle, which is wrong.
1 mark: selects option C, recognising from $\lambda = h/(mv)$ that at equal speed the particle with the greater mass (the neutron) has the shorter de Broglie wavelength

content.text: A ball is launched from a platform at position A with velocity u. It lands in the position shown.

content.alt_text: Side view of a ball launched horizontally from a platform: a ball at point A on top of a platform of height h above a horizontal ground line, a horizontal arrow labelled u leaving A, and a dashed parabolic path curving down to a shaded ball on the ground to the right of a marked point B.

content.text: The ball could be made to land at position B by increasing the
velocity $u$.
launch angle.
mass of the ball.
height of the platform.
Decide first whether B is nearer to or further from the platform than the point where the ball currently lands. That tells you whether the range must increase or decrease.
For a launch from a height, $t = \sqrt{2h/a}$ and the range is $x = u\cos\theta\,t$. Use these to test each of the four proposed changes.
The mass of the ball never appears in the equations of motion, so check that option immediately.
B
Point B is between the base of the platform and the point where the ball currently lands, so the ball must be made to land sooner, that is over a shorter range.

items: Increasing $u$ increases the range, so the ball would overshoot B.
Increasing the height of the platform increases the time of fall and so increases the range.
The mass of the ball cancels out of the equations of projectile motion altogether, so it has no effect on the range.

Tilting the launch so that it has a downward component gives the ball an initial downward velocity, so it reaches the ground sooner and lands short of the present landing point, which is where B lies.

content.text: Of the four, only the launch angle can be changed to reduce the range to the shorter distance to B.

items: 1 mark: selects option B (launch angle), recognising that the range of a projectile launched from a height depends on the launch angle and initial velocity, but is independent of the mass of the ball

content.text: The graph shows the relationship between radiation intensity and wavelength for a black body at 4500 K.

content.alt_text: Graph of Intensity (arbitrary units) against Wavelength (nm) for a black body at 4500 K. The horizontal axis runs from 0 to 2000 nm. The curve is zero below about 200 nm, rises steeply to a smooth peak near 650 nm, then falls away more gradually towards 2000 nm.

content.text: Which statement describes the expected difference in the graph for a black body at 4000 K?
Intensity at all wavelengths will be less.
Intensity at all wavelengths will be greater.
The peak intensity will occur at a higher frequency.
The peak intensity will occur at a shorter wavelength.
A black body radiates a total power proportional to the fourth power of its temperature, $P \propto T^{4}$. Start by asking which of the two temperatures is higher.
Then use Wien's displacement law, $\lambda_{\max}T = \text{constant}$, to work out which way the peak of the curve moves as the temperature falls.
Decide separately whether the whole curve sits lower and where the peak sits, then check the options against both conclusions.
A
The temperature falls from 4500 K to 4000 K. Since the total radiated power varies as $T^{4}$, the cooler black body radiates less energy, and its emitted intensity is lower at every wavelength.
Wien's law also shows that $\lambda_{\max} \propto 1/T$, so the peak of the 4000 K curve moves to a longer wavelength, that is to a lower frequency, and the total area under the curve is smaller.

items: Intensity greater at all wavelengths is wrong because a cooler radiator emits less.
A peak at a higher frequency and a peak at a shorter wavelength both contradict Wien's law, which places the peak at a longer wavelength for a cooler body.
1 mark: selects option A, recognising that a cooler black body radiates less energy at every wavelength and that its peak shifts to a longer wavelength (lower frequency)

content.text: Figure I shows a current flowing through a loop of wire that is in a uniform magnetic field.

content.alt_text: Two perspective drawings of the same rectangular current-carrying loop between the poles of a magnet. In Figure I the loop lies flat, its left side marked X (top) and Y (bottom) with a 'Current' arrow entering the leads; in Figure II the loop has been rotated so that its plane contains the field, with the same X and Y labels and current arrow. Beneath both figures the caption reads 'The loop is then rotated to the position shown in Figure II.'

content.text: The loop is then rotated to the position shown in Figure II. The magnitude of the force on the side XY and the magnitude of the torque on the loop in Figure II are compared to those in Figure I. Which row of the table correctly describes the comparison?
Force in I is greater than in II; torque in I equals torque in II.
Force in I is greater than in II; torque in I is greater than in II.
Force in I equals force in II; torque in I equals torque in II.
Force in I equals force in II; torque in I is greater than torque in II.
Two different quantities are being compared, so reach for two different equations: $F = BIl\sin\theta$ for the force on the wire XY, and $\tau = nIAB\sin\theta$ for the torque on the loop.
For the force, ask what the rotation did to the angle between the current in XY and the field. For the torque, ask what it did to the angle between the field and the normal to the loop.
In Figure I the loop lies flat with the field in its plane; in Figure II it has been turned so that the normal to the loop lies along the field. Work out $\sin\theta$ in each case.
D

The loop is rotated about an axis parallel to the field, so the angle between the current in side XY and the field is unchanged at $90^{\circ}$ in both figures. The force on XY is therefore $BIl$ in both, i.e. the force in I equals the force in II.

The torque behaves differently. In Figure I the loop lies flat, so the field is in the plane of the loop and the area vector is perpendicular to the field: $\tau = nIAB\sin90^{\circ} = nIAB$, the maximum. In Figure II the loop has been turned so that its normal is parallel to the field: $\tau = nIAB\sin0^{\circ} = 0$.
The torque in I is therefore greater than the torque in II, while the forces are equal. That is the last row of the table.

items: Rows showing $I > II$ for the force assume the angle between XY and the field changed, which it did not.
The row showing $I = II$ for the torque is wrong because the torque actually falls to zero in Figure II.

1 mark: selects option D, i.e. the force on side XY is unchanged ($I = II$) because $F = BIl\sin\theta$ still has the full-length conductor perpendicular to the field, while the torque is greater in Figure I than Figure II ($\tau = nIAB\sin\theta$ is zero in II)

content.text: The chart shows part of a nuclear decay series beginning with uranium.

content.alt_text: Decay-series chart with Atomic number on the vertical axis (87 to 92) against Mass number on the horizontal axis (224 to 238). Ra at (88, 226), Th at (90, 230) and U at (92, 238) lie on one descending diagonal line of arrows. content.text: Which option correctly identifies X and Y and the process by which each was produced?
X = ${}^{234}_{90}\mathrm{Th}$, produced by alpha decay;  Y = ${}^{234}_{91}\mathrm{Pa}$, produced by beta decay
X = ${}^{234}_{90}\mathrm{Th}$, produced by alpha decay;  Y = ${}^{234}_{91}\mathrm{Pa}$, produced by alpha decay
X = ${}^{234}_{91}\mathrm{Pa}$, produced by beta decay;  Y = ${}^{234}_{90}\mathrm{Th}$, produced by beta decay
X = ${}^{234}_{91}\mathrm{Pa}$, produced by beta decay;  Y = ${}^{234}_{90}\mathrm{Th}$, produced by alpha decay

On a chart of mass number against atomic number, an alpha decay moves a point 4 to the left in mass number and 2 down in atomic number, while a beta decay keeps the mass number and increases the atomic number by 1, i.e. it is a horizontal arrow.
Follow the arrows leaving the uranium box and read the mass and atomic number off the box each one lands in. Whichever box is reached first identifies X.
Once X is known, the arrow from X to Y tells you what Y is and which decay produced it.
A

From $^{238}_{92}\mathrm{U}$ the arrow that drops 4 in mass number and 2 in atomic number is an alpha decay, and it lands at mass number 234, atomic number 90. That box is X, so $X = {}^{234}_{90}\mathrm{Th}$.
X then decays along a horizontal arrow to the right, keeping the mass number at 234 while the atomic number rises from 90 to 91. That is beta (β⁻) decay, so $Y = {}^{234}_{91}\mathrm{Pa}$.
X is thorium produced by alpha decay and Y is protactinium produced by beta decay, which is the first option.

items: Options that swap the identities of X and Y cannot be right, because X is the box reached directly from uranium.
The option saying Y was produced by alpha decay is wrong, because the arrow from X to Y is horizontal.
1 mark: selects option A, i.e. $X$ is ${}^{234}_{90}\mathrm{Th}$ formed by alpha decay from ${}^{238}_{92}\mathrm{U}$ and $Y$ is ${}^{234}_{91}\mathrm{Pa}$ formed by beta (beta-minus) decay from $X$

content.text: Figure I shows a positively charged particle accelerating freely from X to Y, between oppositely charged plates. The change in the particle's kinetic energy is W. The distance between the plates is then doubled as shown in Figure II. The same charge accelerates from rest over the same distance from X to Y.

content.alt_text: Two parallel-plate diagrams side by side. Figure I: a 1000 V supply across two horizontal plates, the upper plate marked with plus signs and the lower with minus signs, separated by d, with a positive particle X and a downward arrow of length d to point Y. Figure II: the same supply across plates separated by twice the distance, with X and Y still d apart.

content.text: What is the change in kinetic energy of the positively charged particle shown in Figure II?
$\dfrac{W}{2}$
The potential difference across the plates is the same in both figures, but the field strength depends on how far apart the plates are: $E = V/d$.
The work done on the charge over a distance is $W = Fd = qEd$, and that work becomes kinetic energy.
Note that the distance the particle travels from X to Y is the same in both figures. Only the field strength changes.
B

Doubling the plate separation while keeping the 1000 V potential difference halves the field strength. The particle still accelerates over the same distance from X to Y, so the work done on it, and hence its gain in kinetic energy, is half as much: $W_{\mathrm{II}} = qE_{\mathrm{II}}d = \tfrac{1}{2}qE_{\mathrm{I}}d = W/2$.

items: $W$ would be correct only if the field strength were unchanged, and $2W$ would require a stronger field.
The printed paper lists $W$ as both option A and option C, so neither can be the answer.

1 mark: selects option B, i.e. $\tfrac{W}{2}$, recognising that doubling the plate separation at constant potential difference halves the field strength ($E = V/d$) while the distance travelled is unchanged, so $W = qEd = qE'd$ is halved

content.text: Nucleus X has a greater binding energy than nucleus Y. What can be deduced about X and Y?
X is more stable than Y.
Y is more stable than X.
X has a greater mass defect than Y.
Y has a greater mass defect than X.
Binding energy and mass defect are two measures of the same thing, related by a single equation.
Write down the mass-energy relationship and identify which of its terms is the mass defect.
Then ask which of the four statements follows directly from that equation, rather than needing extra assumptions.
C

The mass defect is the mass that appears to be missing from a nucleus compared with its free protons and neutrons, and by $E = \Delta mc^{2}$ it equals the binding energy divided by $c^{2}$. The two are not independent: the larger the binding energy, the larger the mass defect.
So X, with the greater binding energy, has the greater mass defect.

content.text: Planet X has a mass 4 times that of Earth and a radius 3 times that of Earth. The escape velocity at the surface of Earth is $11.2\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}$. What is the escape velocity at the surface of planet X?
Write the escape velocity in terms of the mass $M$ and radius $r$ of the planet: $v_{\text{esc}} = \sqrt{2GM/r}$.

content.text: What evidence resulting from investigations into the photoelectric effect is consistent with the model of light subsequently proposed by Einstein?
Photoelectrons were only ejected from a metal if the light was less than a specific wavelength.
Increasing the intensity of light on a metal increased the maximum kinetic energy of the photoelectrons.
If photons had sufficient energy to eject photoelectrons from a metal, the maximum kinetic energy was independent of the type of metal used.
The probability of photoelectrons being emitted from a metal was proportional to the duration of exposure to light for any given wavelength used.
Einstein's model treats light as photons, each of energy $E = hf$, and a photoelectron is ejected only if that energy exceeds the work function of the metal.
Each option is a piece of experimental evidence. Ask which one the classical wave model of light could NOT explain, because only a quantum description predicts it.
A threshold wavelength is the same idea as a threshold frequency. Think about what happens to the photoelectrons on the long-wavelength side of it, whatever the intensity.
A

A fixed threshold frequency, equivalently a maximum wavelength, exists because each photon delivers its energy in one lump. If the light is longer in wavelength than the threshold, $hf < \phi$ for every photon and no photoelectrons are emitted, however intense the light is. That is only explicable if light consists of photons, so it is the evidence consistent with Einstein's model.

items: B is not evidence: the maximum kinetic energy depends on the frequency, not the intensity; increasing the intensity raises the number of photoelectrons emitted per second.
C is not evidence: $E_{k\max} = hf - \phi$ and $\phi$ differs between metals, so at a fixed frequency the maximum kinetic energy does depend on the metal.
D describes behaviour that a wave model also predicts and so does not single out the photon model.

1 mark: selects option A, i.e. the existence of a threshold wavelength (equivalently a threshold frequency) below which no photoelectrons are emitted, which is only explained by light consisting of photons whose energy $E = hf$ must exceed the work function

content.text: In a thought experiment, two identical parallel aluminium rods, X and Y, are carrying electric currents of equal magnitude. Rod X rests on a table. Rod Y remains stationary, vertically above X, as a result of the magnetic interaction. The masses of the connecting wires are negligible.
Which statement must be correct if rod Y is stationary?

content.alt_text: Printed diagram of two parallel aluminium rods X and Y, connected by wires, with rod X resting on a table and rod Y vertically above it.

content.text: The magnetic force acting on X is upward.
The currents through X and Y are in the same direction.
The force the table exerts on X is equal and opposite to the total weight of X and Y.
The force the table exerts on X is equal and opposite to the force of gravity acting on Y.
Treat the two rods together as one system and list the forces acting on that system from outside it.
The system is stationary, so the resultant force on it is zero. The internal magnetic force between the rods cancels out of that sum.
Which forces on the combined system act vertically? The weight of which bodies must the table be supporting?
C

Consider the two rods as a single system. The forces acting on it from outside are the normal force from the table, which acts upwards on rod X, the total weight of both rods acting downwards, and the magnetic force between them, which is equal and opposite on each rod and so is internal to the chosen system.

The system is stationary, so the vertical forces must balance. The magnetic force is horizontal and cannot support the rods vertically, so the force the table exerts on X must be equal and opposite to the total weight of X and Y.

items: The magnetic force on X must be downwards, not upwards: it balances the upward magnetic repulsion on Y, which is what holds Y up.
For the rods to repel, the currents must be in opposite directions, not the same direction.
The table must support the weight of X as well as Y, so the force from the table is greater than, not equal to, the weight of Y alone.

content.text: A mass attached to a lightweight, rigid arm hanging from point O, oscillates freely between X and Z.
Which statement best describes the torque acting on the arm as it oscillates?

content.alt_text: Printed pendulum diagram showing a lightweight arm pivoted at O, with the mass at X and Z on dashed arcs and at Y directly below the pivot.

content.text: It is constant in magnitude and direction.
It is zero at Y and a maximum at X and Z.
It is zero at X and Z and a maximum at Y.
It is constant in magnitude but its direction changes.
The only force that can turn the arm is the weight of the mass, and it always acts vertically downwards through the centre of mass.
Use $\tau = rF\sin\theta$ with $\theta$ the angle between the arm and the vertical, which is the direction of the weight.
Consider the arm at the lowest point of the swing, and then at the extreme positions at each end of the swing.
B

At Y the arm hangs vertically, so the weight acts along the arm and its line of action passes through the pivot O. Here $\theta = 0$, $\sin\theta = 0$ and the torque is zero. This is also the point where the speed is greatest, which is the usual distractor.
At X and Z the arm is at its greatest angle to the vertical, so $\sin\theta$ is at its maximum and the torque is at its maximum. The speed there is zero, not the torque.
The torque is therefore zero at Y and a maximum at X and Z. It also reverses direction every half swing, so it is not constant in magnitude or direction.

items: 1 mark: selects option B, recognising that the torque about O due to the weight of the mass ($\tau = rF\sin\theta$) is zero when the arm hangs vertically at Y and is a maximum at the extreme positions X and Z

content.alt_text: Option A: the 'Wire X' bar shows three widely spaced plus signs bunched towards the ends of the wire while the 'Wire Y' bar below still shows six evenly spaced plus signs.
Option B: the 'Wire X' bar shows ten closely spaced plus signs crowded together while the 'Wire Y' bar below shows six evenly spaced plus signs.

content.text: Take each wire in turn in the new frame of reference: the positive carriers of wire Y are stationary in this frame, but the positive carriers of wire X are moving, and faster than they are in the laboratory frame.

A moving cloud of like charges is length-contracted, so the carriers in that wire appear closer together (more carriers in the same length), while carriers that are at rest keep their original spacing.
B

In the frame of reference of a positive charge in wire Y, the positive carriers of wire Y are at rest. Their spacing is therefore exactly as in the neutral wires of the stimulus, so wire Y must still show the original evenly spaced carriers.

The conventional currents in the two wires are equal and opposite. In a frame travelling with the positive carriers of wire Y, the positive carriers of wire X must move at the sum of the two current speeds, so they move faster than they do in the laboratory frame.

The faster those carriers travel in this frame, the more their spacing is length-contracted, so more of them are seen in the same length of wire X. The correct diagram therefore shows the carriers of wire X crowded together while wire Y keeps its evenly spaced carriers.

The distractors fail on the frame used: a diagram with wire X spread out would require the observer to be travelling with wire X, and one with wire Y crowded would require the observer to travel with wire Y's carriers in the direction of wire X's current. Only one wire's carriers can be at rest in the observer's frame.

content.text: In 1995, observational evidence showed that Hubble's description of the expansion of the universe was inaccurate. It was discovered that the expansion of the universe was accelerating. This discovery was based on observations of light from galaxies whose distances from Earth could be accurately measured, and were significantly more distant than any observed by Hubble. Which graph relating velocities of galaxies to their distances from Earth is consistent with an accelerating rate of expansion of the universe?

content.alt_text: Option A: a graph with Distance on the horizontal axis and Velocity on the vertical axis, showing a straight line through the origin with a small constant gradient.
Option B: a graph with Distance on the horizontal axis and Velocity on the vertical axis, showing a straight line through the origin with a large constant gradient.

Option C: a graph with Distance on the horizontal axis and Velocity on the vertical axis, showing a curve that starts at the origin with a steep gradient and becomes progressively less steep, approaching the horizontal.
Option D: a graph with Distance on the horizontal axis and Velocity on the vertical axis, showing a curve that starts at the origin with a shallow gradient and becomes progressively steeper.

content.text: The gradient of a velocity-distance graph is the recession velocity gained per unit distance. Ask what the gradient was at the time the light was emitted, not what it is today.

Light from the most distant galaxies left them longest ago. If the expansion is accelerating, the expansion rate was smaller in the past, so those galaxies are seen moving more slowly than a straight-line (non-accelerating) Hubble graph would predict.
D

We do not observe the universe as it is now; we observe the most distant galaxies as they were when the light left them. That light has been travelling the longest time, so it was emitted when the universe was younger and the expansion rate was lower than the present rate.

For an accelerating expansion the observed recession velocity therefore increases with distance more slowly than the straight line through the origin that a non-accelerating (Hubble) universe would give. The gradient of the graph must decrease with distance, approaching a limiting value, rather than increasing.
This eliminates the two straight lines through the origin, which describe a constant expansion rate, and the curve whose gradient increases with distance, which describes a decelerating expansion.

The engines change one thing only, the speed, and everything else follows from conservation of energy. At each point decide which of the three quantities — kinetic energy, gravitational potential energy and total mechanical energy — are already fixed by the stem and which must be calculated.

For part (a) no numbers are needed. After the firing the satellite is moving further from Earth, so decide which energy store must be growing and which must be shrinking, and be careful that the total is only constant once the engine is shut down.

content.text: Analyse qualitatively the energy changes as the satellite moves from P to Q.

No calculation is needed. Use two facts: the engine is now off, so nothing is doing work on the satellite; and the engines pushed it faster along its direction of travel at P, so it now has more total energy than it did in the circular orbit.

Between P and Q the radius is increasing. Decide which of the two energy stores must grow as the satellite climbs further from Earth, and use conservation to say what happens to the other one. The total tells you nothing about the split, so do not use it to argue the two stores are unchanged.
The kinetic energy decreases and the gravitational potential energy increases, consistent with the law of conservation of energy; the total mechanical energy stays constant.
As the satellite moves, its kinetic energy decreases and is transformed into an increasing gravitational potential energy, consistent with the law of conservation of energy.

content.text: Show that the kinetic energy of the satellite at Q is $1.194 \times 10^{10}\,\mathrm{J}$.

Two quantities have to be in hand before the kinetic energy can be found: the total mechanical energy of the satellite at Q, and its gravitational potential energy at Q. Remember that the engine's contribution is added to the total, not to the kinetic energy directly.

The potential energy at Q needs the radius of Q, not the radius of the original circular orbit, and it needs the Earth's mass, which is not in the stem and must be taken from the data sheet. Then use $E = U + K$ with the total at Q.

content.text: Explain the motion of the satellite after it passes through Q.

Convert the kinetic energy at Q into a speed with $K = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^{2}$, then work out what speed a circular orbit at that same radius would require using $v_{\text{orbit}} = \sqrt{GM/r}$ and the Earth's mass from the data sheet. The comparison of those two numbers settles the question.

Keep the two speeds clearly labelled, because the whole argument turns on which is larger. A satellite whose speed exceeds the circular value at its radius has too much energy to be captured into that circle, so its distance from Earth continues to increase rather than staying constant.

As it passes Q the satellite's velocity ($7.727 \times 10^{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$) exceeds the velocity required for a circular orbit at that radius ($7.644 \times 10^{3}\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$), so it continues on its trajectory, increasing its distance from Earth.
i.e. $v_{Q} > v_{\text{req}}$. This means the satellite will continue on its trajectory increasing its distance from Earth.
